 Editorial | 12 hours ago Sourcing from the US makes LPG costlier
 FE
 Published :
 Nov 14, 2026, 17:48 
 The slight easing of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices over the past week has brought some relief to households. A 12-kilogram cylinder now sells for around Tk 2,100 to Tk 2,400, depending on the brand, down from the staggering Tk 2,550 consumers were paying just days ago. This drop feels like a small victory, but in truth, it barely scratches the surface of the problem. The official rate fixed by the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) stands at Tk 2,060, which means even after the much-publicised market monitoring drive the gap still remains wide. Although the gap has momentarily narrowed somewhat, the continued overcharging says much about the government's failure to enforce its own pricing decisions. This is a matter of concern for more than 10 million consumers, most of them households, who depend on LPG for cooking, particularly after the suspension of new household gas connections pushed many families towards cylinders. Surveillance has reportedly been expanded through deputy commissioners' offices and consumer rights drives, but the results are visible only at the edges of the market. Information and Broadcasting Adviser Dr Zahed Ur Rahman has recently blamed traders' speculative practices for the higher prices. While such practices may well be part of the problem, his explanation leaves out another important factor that has a direct bearing on the price consumers end up paying. 
 Indeed, one of the major reasons behind the high cost is the change in import sources toward the United States. Bangladesh has traditionally relied heavily on Middle Eastern suppliers, but the tables turned once the reciprocal trade agreement signed with the US facilitated purchases of American energy worth $15 billion dollars over the course of next 15 years. Disrupted shipping routes amid the conflict involving the US, Israel and Iran have no doubt added to the strain, though the pledge itself did much of the heavy lifting. In September, US-based firms accounted for over 80 per cent of Bangladesh's LPG imports compared with 27.4 per cent a year earlier. Private importers since then rushed to honour the commitment, resulting in gas making a far longer route. Longer voyages mean higher freight and insurance, and cargoes bought on American export terms leave little room for hard bargaining. Some economists had warned that such commitments would narrow the freedom to buy from the cheapest source, and events have since proved them right. 
 When neighbouring India sells the same product for around Tk 1,200, it becomes clear that Bangladesh is paying a premium due to its procurement strategy. India produces a good deal of LPG at home, buys the rest through large government owned companies and keeps household prices under official watch. Bangladesh has done the opposite. Nearly 99 per cent of the market is in private hands and the state company supplies barely 1 per cent, giving a handful of businesses considerable influence over the import, storage, bottling and distribution. 
 In such a market, regulation certainly cannot be limited to announcing a monthly or quarterly price and expecting everyone to comply. At the very least, BERC must independently verify the import costs submitted by operators and ensure that every increase in freight, insurance, procurement premiums and other expenses is properly supported by documents. The government also needs to take a hard look at the growing dependence on US-based suppliers and weigh whether a more diversified sourcing strategy can bring import costs down. Any energy purchase commitment arising from the reciprocal trade agreement must be tested against the interests of domestic consumers instead of being pursued without considering their financial consequences.
